parts.description: A trapezoidal stainless steel box grater with perforated faces, black rubberized plastic handle and base trim, and a translucent plastic collection drawer.
parts.reasoning: Estimated as a medium kitchen box grater approximately 0.24 m tall with a 0.13 m x 0.10 m base footprint and a narrower top. The visible structure is mostly thin stainless steel sheet with added plastic/rubber handle, base trim, and a small translucent plastic drawer. A typical object of this size and construction is about 0.4-0.6 kg; 0.50 kg is a realistic working mass including the metal shell, molded handle/base, and drawer. Because the collision representation should be a simplified solid envelope rather than the true thin sheet volume, the density is set as an effective bulk density of about 170 kg/m^3, not stainless steel's material density of ~7850 kg/m^3. This produces the correct mass when using convex decomposition over the occupied volume. The resting contact is mostly the black rubberized/plastic base trim, so friction is higher than bare stainless steel: static friction is estimated at 0.75 and dynamic friction at 0.60. Restitution is kept low at 0.30 because the object is a hollow metal/plastic assembly that may ring or rattle but should not bounce strongly. For Isaac Sim/PhysX, convex decomposition is preferred over a single convex hull because the handle opening, recessed drawer area, flared trapezoidal body, and base trim are meaningfully non-convex. The many grater holes should generally be ignored in collision for performance and contact stability; representing every perforation would create excessive tiny contact patches and unstable snagging. If exact interaction with holes or sharp blades is required, a separate high-resolution SDF mesh may be used, but this is much more expensive for a dynamic rigid body. Recommended rest offset is 0.0 m and contact offset is about 0.003 m, small enough to avoid visible floating while still generating robust contacts on a 20-25 cm object. Initial velocity is zero. CCD is disabled by default for performance because the object is not expected to be fast-moving and the simplified colliders have finite thickness; enable CCD if it is dropped, thrown, or moved above roughly 1-2 m/s near thin obstacles. Mild compliant contact values are suggested only to approximate the rubberized base and reduce chatter; they can be disabled for a purely rigid metal collider. For stable robotic/contact-rich scenes, 60 Hz is acceptable, while 120 Hz may be preferable if grasping the handle or interacting with the drawer recess. A practical sleep threshold would be low/default so the object hibernates after settling; avoid overly large thresholds because the low mass and narrow base can otherwise freeze small rocking motions prematurely.
